extracted.intended_audience: Prospective European Research Council (ERC) Starting Grant applicants; early-career researchers (≈2–7 years post-PhD) preparing ERC SG proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance on preparing and writing a competitive ERC Starting Grant application, including eligibility/timing, crafting the B1/B2 proposal and CV to demonstrate independence, preparing preliminary data, and performing at the interview (Stage 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility window and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who is between 2 to 7 years post‐PhD is eligible to apply but extensions are also granted for maternity leave, compulsory military service, medical leave, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure, email the ERC for clarification. Be aware of timing consequences: if rejected at Stage 1 (proposal not sent out for review) you are not allowed to apply for the next call — so consider whether to apply late in your eligibility window or to wait and strengthen your record first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 1 assessment focuses on B1 and CV
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the panel will only look at B1 (the five‐page extended synopsis) and your CV at Stage 1, these must stand out as strong and independent documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with writing the B1 (five-page extended synopsis) to clearly summarise key ideas; ensure B1 can stand alone and be re-written when preparing the B2. Pay meticulous attention to detail: the panel decides whether to send your proposal for external review based largely on these items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate independence in the CV
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers answer the question: 'To what extent does the PI provide evidence of creative independent thinking?' Evidence of independence is critical and often decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly highlight any signals of independence in your CV. Strong evidence includes last author (senior) papers without previous advisors, independent funding where you are listed as PI, invited talks, organizing conferences, membership on journal editorial boards, invited papers, single‑authored perspectives, and awards typically given to independent PIs. Even one paper without your PhD advisor is noted as a minimum in guidelines; publish or otherwise obtain visible independent outputs where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project must be high risk/high reward yet feasible for you
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC funds 'frontier research' aiming for fundamental advances; proposals should be high risk/high reward while still being projects the applicant can realistically bring to fruition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance: propose an idea that could change the direction of your field but is within the scope of what you (given your track record/expertise) can achieve. Avoid over‑ambitious projects you cannot credibly deliver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a transformative 'dream' project within your field (Option 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 3: a dream project that, if successful, could change your field — recommended approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best when it is high‑risk, revolutionary, ideally with limited literature (so you avoid offending established experts), and one where you are uniquely the best person to deliver. Preliminary data helps but is not always required; being already recognized in the field strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of continuing previous work (Option 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 1: a project that is a natural continuation of your previous work — can be judged as incremental and raise doubts about your independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If choosing this route, you must convincingly show how the project is ground‑breaking and why your previous advisors cannot perform it. Combine experiences uniquely to avoid perceptions of mere continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of moving into a new area (Option 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 2: a project in an area where you have some experience but are not well known — risks include skepticism from field experts and potential perception of naivety or arrogance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If moving fields, consider generating preliminary data and carefully frame criticisms of existing approaches to avoid alienating experts. Enter areas with limited prior literature where possible to reduce friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing multiple independent reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: An ERC proposal can be evaluated by up to ~12 independent reviewers; even one or two negative comments can cause failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write to a broad scientific audience, anticipate diverse critiques, and remove obvious weaknesses. Remember that 7–10 reviewers is common; design the proposal and CV to be persuasive across that wide reviewer pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offending or alienating reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticising established approaches or literature, especially from the perspective of a junior PI, can be interpreted as naive or arrogant and provoke negative reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame weaknesses of others' approaches tactfully; prefer proposals that do not require overt criticism of prominent researchers' work. When discussing prior work, be constructive and avoid language that could be seen as dismissive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary data: situational importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary data can help demonstrate feasibility and required expertise, particularly if your project is far from your current field or mainstream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain preliminary results when moving into a new area or when feasibility is a likely concern; however, many successful applicants have obtained funding without such data — do not let lack of preliminary data alone deter you from applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to detail and 'advertising' yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC pays close attention to how applicants present themselves; 'attention to detail matters so much' in the CV and proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly highlight achievements that signal independence and excellence (e.g., awards, invited talks, editorial roles). Make it easy for panel/reviewers to notice relevant credentials by calling them out clearly in the CV and proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview (Stage 2) presentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: At Stage 2 you give a 10‑minute presentation followed by 20 minutes of questioning; you do not receive reviewers' comments beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your talk clear about goals and importance, geared to a non‑specialist panel. Summarise key achievements and why you are the best person to do the project. Time your talk for ~9 minutes 40 seconds (screen turns black at 10 minutes), practice with people from your subfield, broader field, and slightly outside, be prepared to present without your own laptop, energize the panel, and be ready to answer questions quickly, confidently, and to the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering questions efficiently in the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: You must respond fast and clearly to panel questions; leaving many reviewer concerns unaddressed is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer quickly and to the point so you can address as many questions as possible; practice concise, confident replies. If you can rebut or clarify a reviewers' misunderstanding, do so assertively (even if unsure), as you have no later opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel's role and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel evaluates reviewers' feedback and applicant performance in the interview; they can compensate for a small number of unfair reviews but cannot overturn many negative reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel support can help mitigate one or two unfair comments, but your overall proposal and CV must still stand up to multiple reviewers. Treat the panel as an ally but don't rely on them to rescue fundamentally weak aspects of your application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic timing of application
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide when to apply based on eligibility years and expected strengthening of your record (e.g., upcoming papers); applying too late risks losing further opportunities if rejected at Stage 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider applying as soon as you are reasonably competitive (even two years from PhD) but weigh whether an extra year of papers or last‑author outputs would materially improve your chances. Use failed attempts to guide timing for subsequent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use failed attempts to improve and persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsuccessful applications are common (≈70% rejected at Stage 1; ≈10% overall success rate) and should be used as learning opportunities to refine proposal and CV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace rejection, learn from reviewer/panel feedback, address weaknesses (e.g., obtain last-author papers), and reapply until successful. Consider alternative funding avenues (consolidator grants, national schemes) along the way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical preparation before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, find and read successful grants in your field, discuss a handful of ideas with specific-field and broader-field colleagues, and research previous awardees (but don't be discouraged by them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain sample funded proposals where possible, discuss ideas across levels of expertise, and craft several related ideas so you can present multiple strong directions. Keep in mind that the panel will evaluate across a broader field than your immediate subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly highlight accomplishments that reviewers outside your subfield might not recognize
rubrics_metrics.description: Some achievements that demonstrate independence within your subfield may be obscure to reviewers from related fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an award or role signals independence but is niche, explain its significance in the CV or proposal so broader reviewers notice its weight (e.g., 'award typically given to independent PIs').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal clarity: clear goal and stated importance
rubrics_metrics.description: No one likes a proposal that does not have a clear goal or that doesn't explain why the work matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state what you will do, why it is important, and how success will change the field. Use presentation and B1 to communicate these points plainly to non-specialist reviewers/panel members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical logistics and presentation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Know logistical quirks of the interview (10-minute countdown display, projector-only possibilities, screen blackout at 10 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice with a 10‑minute countdown to ensure timing; have printed slides or be prepared to present via projector; design the talk to finish slightly early to avoid abrupt cutoff.
